# The Coincidence of Wants is Not Solved

In the potted history of the invention of money, it is often claimed that money solved the illiquidity/improbability issue of the [coincidence of wants](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coincidence_of_wants) problems.

The standard story runs like this. In a barter economy, trade requires a double coincidence: if I have wheat and want shoes, I must find a shoemaker who both wants wheat and has shoes to spare. The odds of such a match are slim, and finding one takes time, so many mutually beneficial trades never happen.

Money is said to dissolve the problem by splitting one transaction into two. I sell my wheat to anyone who wants it, taking money in return, and later spend that money on shoes with anyone who sells them. Neither trade requires the other party to want what I happen to hold. Because everyone accepts money, it works as a common intermediary, and so the shoemaker's appetite for wheat no longer matters.

Money is also divisible and durable, so it can be saved and spent in small amounts. The upshot, as usually told, is that trade becomes faster and cheaper, and exchange can expand.

The thing is though, money only alleviates some of the most common and simple cases of the coincidence of wants. The coincidence of wants is basically an arbitrarily complex class of problems. Take for instance spectrum auctions:

Governments license slices of radio spectrum to mobile carriers, but a carrier's value for one license often depends on which others it wins. A license covering one city is worth far more alongside the neighboring regions (complements), while two licenses for the same area may be substitutes. Money and a simple sealed bid don't solve this. If I bid on a bundle and lose one piece, I'm stuck with fragments worth much less than I paid. In the 1990s, Paul Milgrom and Robert Wilson designed the simultaneous multiple-round auction, in which bidders see prices and adjust their bids across many licenses at once. Later formats allow bids on whole packages. The mechanism is really a heavy computation for discovering who wants which combination. The work earned them the 2020 Nobel in economics. See the [overview of spectrum auctions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_auction).

Or kidney transplant chains:

Patients who need a kidney often have a willing living donor who is medically incompatible with them, by blood type or tissue match. Money can't fix that, since organ sales are illegal and the problem is matching, not price. In a transplant chain, an altruistic donor with no particular recipient gives a kidney to a patient in one incompatible pair. That pair's donor then gives to the next pair's patient, and so on, until the last donor gives to someone on the deceased-donor waiting list or starts a new chain. Each patient gets a compatible kidney, and no one needs a direct swap. Finding the best chains across a large pool is a hard computational problem, which Alvin Roth and colleagues helped solve with matching algorithms. See the [overview of kidney paired donation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kidney_paired_donation).

Or take the extreme case of a dating situation where two people really like each other but are never single at the same time. In rom-coms, this takes a deus ex machina to solve.

There are many other such cases where money is necessary but not sufficient for solving a coincidence of wants problem. There are both additional conditions and more complex computations.

In many ways, we only ever solved a narrow class of triage problems in the larger coincidence of wants design space. In general, the money-based market only satisfies demands with “assembly required.”

One of the most intractable classes of coincidence of wants problems is labor markets. You have services to sell. I need those services. We agree on price and trust each other. What’s stopping us transacting? Typically the issue is *availability and need schedules of time and money.* I want 10 hours right now but can only pay you a month from now. You can only give me 3 hours now, and 7 hours in 6 weeks, but you need 5 hours worth of payment right away.

We try to solve this sort of problem with interest-driven credit markets, where money itself has a price calibrated to risk. But here, the fact that a distant bank doesn’t trust either of us much might add a lot of cost to the transaction. Cost that exceeds the risk between just the two of us. 

Add any sort of risk and it gets worse fast. Maybe I am buying your services to build a speculative product, and you want to share in the risk for more upside. The cost of capital now goes even higher.

Now, community cooperative small-capital markets can help, since they know more about transacting parties and can charge less. But in general they are starved of liquidity. DeFi in crypto showed that this problem can be partly solved but at the cost of dealing in shitcoin economies to represent all the latent transactional potential, adding to the structural risk. There is a shittiness-liquidity tradeoff. At one extreme you and I underwrite our transaction with a shitcoin nobody else wants. This does nothing to improve the situation. But if a third person likes us both and participates in the shitcoin market, they could potentially enable our transaction at a lower cost than a bank.

All thus to say, money is merely a crude first solution to the simplest class of coincidence of wants problems. The vast majority of valuable potential transactions never happen not because of “inefficient” markets (ie poor information flows and weak price discovery) but because the coincidence of wants problem is too hard.
